summaries.example: Imagine a school history book that names many famous men but almost no women. Students might ask, “What did the women do and think?” Latin American feminist thinkers ask a similar question about history. They look for women’s ideas in books, poems, songs, family stories, and community memories. They also ask whether every girl and woman has the same experience, since race, class, language, religion, sexuality, and community can shape people’s lives differently.
summaries.summary: Latin American feminism grew from the histories and everyday lives of people in Latin America and the Caribbean. These histories include colonial rule, the enslavement of African peoples, and the marginalization of Indigenous peoples. Feminist thinkers have questioned rules that treat men as the standard for all human beings and have worked for women’s education, political participation, fair work, bodily freedom, and social justice. The tradition is not one single view. Different women and groups have disagreed about whether to work with political parties, governments, or organizations, and about which problems deserve the most attention. Later thinkers especially criticized versions of feminism that centered mostly white, middle-class, heterosexual women. Indigenous, Afro-descended, lesbian, and other voices emphasized that identity is complex and that community, race, class, sexuality, and colonial history matter. The entry also explains that women’s thinking has appeared in philosophy, literature, songs, oral histories, activism, and labor movements. Recovering these ideas changes what counts as philosophy and who is remembered as a thinker.
key_ideas: Latin American feminism has many histories and viewpoints, so it is often better understood as many feminisms.
Women’s ideas appeared long before the organized movements of the 1960s and 1970s, but history often left them out.
Feminist thought is connected to daily life, including education, work, family, health, political rights, and safety.
Race, class, ethnicity, sexuality, religion, and community can affect women differently; one idea cannot describe everyone’s experience.
Ideas can change when they travel between countries, languages, and communities.
Latin American feminist philosophy connects thinking with action to change unfair social conditions.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because history and philosophy can leave people out. Learning about Latin American feminisms helps us notice women as knowledge-makers and political actors. It also teaches that fairness requires listening to people whose lives are different, rather than assuming one solution works for everyone. The tradition shows how ideas can grow from ordinary experiences and community struggles.

important_terms.definition: A way of thinking and acting that questions unfair treatment of women and supports changes that help women live with freedom and respect.
The belief that people should be able to make important choices about their own lives and bodies.
The study of how people’s ideas and lives are shaped by their time, place, and history.
A system in which men or male-centered rules have more power, often making women’s lives less equal.
The work of carrying an idea from one language or place into another, where its meaning may change.

questions_to_think_about: Whose ideas are missing from the history books you read?
Why might two women from different communities have different goals?
What can happen when an idea changes as it moves into a new language or place?
How can learning about the past help people make fairer choices today?

summaries.example: Suppose an international organization introduces a policy called “gender empowerment” to a local women’s group. The phrase may sound useful, but the group might ask whose definition of empowerment is being used, which language shaped it, and whether it addresses local problems such as land loss, racism, poverty, or community safety. One group may favor working with the government to change policy; another may worry that institutions will soften or control the movement’s original demands. The disagreement illustrates debates about translation, autonomy, institutionalization, and complex identity.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry describes Latin American feminism, including Caribbean feminism, as a plural and historically situated field of political theory, social activism, and philosophy. Its background includes colonialism, the enslavement of African peoples, the marginalization of Indigenous peoples, changing economic systems, and political repression. The entry traces feminist ideas from earlier writers and oral traditions through early twentieth-century campaigns for education, labor rights, equality, and suffrage; the “years of silence,” when women participated in politics and produced literature without always making explicit feminist demands; and the movements of the 1970s–1990s. Those movements addressed bodily autonomy, reproductive rights, motherhood, violence, militarism, democratization, labor, and social services. Regional Encuentros made disagreements visible, especially between autonomous feminists and party-affiliated activists. In the 1990s, feminism increasingly entered NGOs, public policy, universities, and international institutions. This institutionalization expanded resources and recognition but was criticized for adapting feminism to neoliberal policies and weakening attention to structural inequality. Twenty-first-century dissident voices challenged dominant models centered on white or mestiza, middle-class, heterosexual experiences. Decolonial, Indigenous, Afro-descended, and lesbian feminisms emphasized that gender is inseparable from race, class, sexuality, community, and colonial history. The entry presents philosophy as part of this political work: recovering women’s intellectual contributions changes the boundaries of the philosophical canon.
key_ideas: The entry presents a genealogy: feminist ideas existed before the movements commonly dated to the 1960s and 1970s, including arguments for women’s education, equality, labor rights, and political participation.
The history is heterogeneous because colonialism, racial hierarchies, class relations, military regimes, democratization, religion, and local political conditions differed across the region.
Late twentieth-century movements connected women’s liberation to bodily autonomy, reproductive rights, resistance to state repression, and challenges to the division between public and private life.

Autonomy produced a recurring disagreement between independent feminists and activists working through political parties or other institutions; later models explored cooperation without surrendering a feminist position.
The movement of concepts such as gender from North America and Europe raised questions about translation, unequal knowledge flows, and whether imported categories fit local conditions.
Contemporary Indigenous, Afro-descended, lesbian, and decolonial critiques challenge a supposedly universal feminism that overlooks race, class, sexuality, community, and coloniality.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry matters because it shows that feminist philosophy is not produced from one universal location. Knowledge is shaped by language, history, institutions, and power. Its account also warns against treating “women” as a single, unified group when colonialism, racism, class inequality, sexuality, and community belonging produce different forms of subordination and resistance. Studying these debates helps readers evaluate both the benefits and limits of universal categories, institutional reform, and political alliances.

important_terms.definition: A field of thought and political practice that examines women’s subordination and seeks social transformation; in this tradition, it includes multiple, sometimes conflicting positions.
A contested commitment to maintaining a feminist standpoint and avoiding control by parties, states, NGOs, or funding agencies; it can also involve engaged cooperation.
The process by which concepts and political ideas move across languages, regions, and institutions, acquiring altered meanings through unequal power relations.
A social system and set of power relations that organizes authority around male dominance and helps explain women’s subordination.
An approach that examines how gender interacts with race, ethnicity, class, sexuality, religion, and community rather than treating identity as one-dimensional.
A critical approach that studies how colonial histories continue to shape knowledge, identity, power, and social institutions.
The process by which activism becomes organized through universities, NGOs, governments, and other formal institutions, sometimes expanding influence and sometimes reducing radical critique.

questions_to_think_about: When does cooperation with a government or political party strengthen a movement, and when might it limit that movement’s independence?
Can a concept remain the same when it crosses languages and political contexts? Why or why not?
Why is womanhood alone insufficient for explaining all women’s experiences in this tradition?
How can recovering oral histories change the accepted history of philosophy?
What might a decolonial approach require from feminist theory and practice?

summaries.example: A group of students wants to improve safety and fairness in its town. One student thinks the group should join a political party. Another wants it to stay independent so its goals will not be pushed aside. A third says the plan must include Indigenous families, Afro-descended families, poor workers, and different kinds of families, because “all women” do not face the same problems. Their discussion mirrors debates in Latin American feminisms about autonomy, inclusion, class, race, sexuality, and working with institutions.
summaries.summary: Latin American feminism is a broad tradition of ideas and movements shaped by the histories of Latin America and the Caribbean. The entry connects those histories to colonialism, the enslavement of African peoples, the marginalization of Indigenous peoples, economic change, and political repression. It explains that feminist thinking began before the organized movements of the 1960s and 1970s. Earlier writers and activists supported women’s education, intellectual life, equality, workers’ rights, and political participation. During the twentieth century, women also expressed feminist ideas through literature, labor organizing, social movements, and oral traditions. From the 1970s through the 1990s, movements challenged military regimes and patriarchy, defended bodily autonomy and reproductive rights, and organized around health, education, work, and freedom from violence. Regional feminist meetings revealed disagreements about autonomy, political-party membership, socialism, and the meaning of feminist organizing. Later, feminism became more connected to NGOs, universities, governments, and international policy. Some saw this as useful, while others worried it made activism less radical and increased inequality between groups. In the twenty-first century, Indigenous, Afro-descended, lesbian, and decolonial thinkers criticized versions of feminism that treated women as one uniform group. They argued that gender must be understood together with race, class, sexuality, ethnicity, colonial history, and community. The entry also presents Latin American feminist philosophy as a field that links theory with political practice and recovers women who were overlooked in standard histories of philosophy.
key_ideas: Latin American feminism has never been just one movement; different regions and groups developed different priorities.
Earlier women thinkers and activists argued for education, political rights, workers’ rights, and equality before the better-known movements of the 1960s and 1970s.
In the 1970s and 1980s, activists connected women’s freedom to bodily autonomy, reproductive rights, opposition to military repression, and social justice.
Some feminists valued independence from political parties and institutions, while others believed feminist goals should be connected to wider struggles against class oppression.
As feminist work entered NGOs, universities, governments, and international programs, it gained influence but could also lose attention to local needs and deeper causes of inequality.
Later critics argued that feminism must take race, ethnicity, class, sexuality, colonial history, and community seriously.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it expands our understanding of who creates knowledge and how social change happens. It shows that feminism can include disagreements rather than a single program. It also encourages careful listening: a policy that helps one group may not address another group’s history or needs. By studying these ideas, we can better understand how power shapes identity, language, institutions, and the writing of history.

important_terms.definition: A group of ideas and actions that challenges unfair treatment of women and seeks greater freedom, equality, and social change.
Independence in making choices and setting goals, especially without being controlled by a political party, government, or funder.
The historical study of how a set of ideas develops over time, including the people and movements that shaped it.
A system of social power in which men and male-centered rules are treated as more important, often subordinating women.
The way ideas change when they move between languages, countries, communities, or institutions.
The process of placing feminist work into formal organizations such as universities, NGOs, governments, or policy programs.
An approach that challenges the continuing effects of colonial rule on knowledge, identity, and power.

questions_to_think_about: Why might feminists disagree about whether to work with a political party?
What is gained and lost when a social movement becomes part of an institution?
Why might the same feminist idea mean something different in two countries?
How do race, class, sexuality, or community change a person’s experience of being treated unfairly?
Why is it important to find women’s ideas in oral history, literature, and activism as well as philosophy books?
